Compare BLIP-2 and Flamingo on vision encoder using only the prepared corpus.

## vision encoder · Side-by-side claims

### blip-2-2301.12597v1

Requirement: `req_9a9be430e5ba45bff83d6a3ce1a4d2ed` · Status: `verified`

BLIP-2 uses a frozen pre-trained image encoder; it explores two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: ViT-L/14 from CLIP and ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP.
The image encoder is frozen pre-trained, and BLIP-2 removes the last layer of the ViT, using the second-to-last layer's output features.
BLIP-2 uses the second-to-last layer's output features of the ViT as the image encoder output, which leads to slightly better performance.

Claim: `claim_5e39bc27f05e7443e7a9f39bfdf26e96`

Sources:

- `ev_9331722f1a47399ab173e624d02c6985` · blip-2-2301.12597v1 · Page 4

### flamingo-2204.14198v1

Requirement: `req_fc4e37577cfdbaec487b0362bdba1d67` · Status: `verified`

Flamingo's vision encoder is a pretrained Normalizer-Free ResNet (NFNet), specifically the F6 model.
The Flamingo vision encoder is pretrained with a contrastive objective (à la CLIP) on image-text pairs, using a two-term contrastive loss with mean-pooled image encoder output and mean-pooled BERT output; during main Flamingo training the vision encoder weights are frozen.
The vision encoder's role is to extract semantic spatial features (color, shape, nature, positions of objects); its final stage output is a 2D spatial grid of features X_f, to which a learnt temporal position encoding is added before flattening and concatenation, feeding the Perceiver Resampler.

evidence.text: Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

The vision encoder's role is to extract semantic spatial features (color, shape, nature, positions of objects); its final stage output is a 2D spatial grid of features X_f, to which a learnt temporal position encoding is added before flattening and concatenation, feeding the Perceiver Resampler.

evidence.text: Vision encoder: from pixels to features. Our model’s vision encoder is a pretrained Normalizer- Free ResNet (NFNet) (Brock et al., 2021) – we use the F6 model. We chose this family of visual backbones thanks to their excellent trade-oﬀbetween performance and eﬃciency given our hardware. We pretrain the vision encoder using a contrastive objective on our datasets of image and text pairs,

The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

using the two-term contrastive loss from Radford et al. (2021). Contrastive similarities are computed as the dot product of the mean pooling of the image encoder output, and the mean pooled output of a BERT model (Devlin et al., 2018). The performance of our contrastive pretrained model is given in Section 4.2.3 and more details about the contrastive training are given in Appendix C.2.2. During the main training phase of the Flamingo models, we leave the vision encoder frozen as it performs favorably when compared to training the vision model directly from our text generation objective (see ablations in Section 4.4). The output of the ﬁnal stage is a 2D spatial grid of features 𝑋𝑓, which

𝑋𝑓. These visual features are obtained by ﬁrst adding a learnt temporal position encoding to each spatial grid of features corresponding to a given frame of the video (an image being considered as a single-frame video). Note that we only use temporal encodings and no spatial grid position encodings; we did not observe improvements from the latter, potentially because CNNs implicitly encode space information channel-wise (Islam et al., 2021). The visual features are then ﬂattened and concatenated as illustrated in Figure 4. The number of output tokens of the Resampler is thus equal to the number of learnt latent queries. Unlike in DETR and Perceiver, the keys and values computed from the learnt latents are concatenated to the keys and values obtained from 𝑋𝑓, which we found to perform slightly better. We show later in the ablation studies (Section 4.4), that using such a vision-language resampler module outperforms a plain transformer and an MLP. More architectural details are provided in Table 13.

The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

evidence.text: Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

The cost of vision-and-language pre-training has become increasingly prohibitive due to end-to- end training of large-scale models. This paper proposes BLIP-2, a generic and efﬁcient pre- training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language mod- els. BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a lightweight Querying Transformer, which is pre- trained in two stages. The ﬁrst stage boot- straps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision- language tasks, despite having signiﬁcantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer train- able parameters. We also demonstrate the model’s emerging capabilities of zero-shot image-to-text generation that can follow natural language in- structions.

• BLIP-2 effectively leverages both frozen pre-trained im- age models and language models. We bridge the modality gap using a Q-Former pre-trained in two-stages: repre- sentation learning stage and generative learning stage. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks including visual question answer- ing, image captioning, and image-text retrieval.

• Due to the use of frozen unimodal models and a lightweight Q-Former, BLIP-2 is more compute-efﬁcient than exisiting state-of-the-arts. For example, BLIP-2 out- performs Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54× fewer trainable pa- rameters. Furthermore, our results show that BLIP-2 is a generic method that can harvest more advanced unimodal models for better VLP performance.

We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

Requirement: `req_9b812a56c386edc56b01ad7612222137` · Status: `verified`

BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a Querying Transformer (Q-Former), a lightweight module that is the trainable connector between a frozen image encoder and a frozen LLM; it is pre-trained in two stages.

The Q-Former uses 32 learnable queries of dimension 768; its output query representation Z (32x768) is a bottleneck much smaller than the frozen image features (e.g., 257x1024 for ViT-L/14), forcing the queries to extract visual information most relevant to the text.

evidence.text: We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

• Due to the use of frozen unimodal models and a lightweight Q-Former, BLIP-2 is more compute-efﬁcient than exisiting state-of-the-arts. For example, BLIP-2 out- performs Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54× fewer trainable pa- rameters. Furthermore, our results show that BLIP-2 is a generic method that can harvest more advanced unimodal models for better VLP performance.

• BLIP-2 effectively leverages both frozen pre-trained im- age models and language models. We bridge the modality gap using a Q-Former pre-trained in two-stages: repre- sentation learning stage and generative learning stage. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks including visual question answer- ing, image captioning, and image-text retrieval.

In our experiments, we use 32 queries where each query has a dimension of 768 (same as the hidden dimension of the Q-Former). We use Z to denote the output query representation. The size of Z (32 × 768) is much smaller than the size of frozen image features (e.g. 257 × 1024 for ViT-L/14). This bottleneck architecture works together with our pre-training objectives into forcing the queries to extract visual information that is most relevant to the text.

• Powered by LLMs (e.g. OPT (Zhang et al., 2022), FlanT5 (Chung et al., 2022)), BLIP-2 can be prompted to perform zero-shot image-to-text generation that follows natural language instructions, which enables emerging capabilities such as visual knowledge reasoning, visual conversation, etc. (see Figure 4 for examples).

Flamingo bridges the frozen vision encoder and frozen LM via two learnable components: a Perceiver Resampler followed by freshly initialised cross-attention layers interleaved between the pretrained LM layers.
The Perceiver Resampler takes a variable number of image or video features from the vision encoder and produces a fixed, small number (64) of visual tokens via learned latent queries fed to a transformer stack that cross-attends to the flattened visual features, reducing the complexity of vision-text cross attention.
The visual tokens condition a frozen LM through freshly initialised cross-attention layers interleaved between pretrained LM layers, letting the LM incorporate visual information for next-token prediction while the language-only self-attention layers are kept frozen.

evidence.text: The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

Second, those visual tokens are used to condition the frozen LM using freshly initialised cross attention layers (Section 3.1.2) that are interleaved between the pretrained LM layers. These new layers oﬀer an expressive way for the LM to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.

It takes as input a variable number of image or video features from the vision encoder and produces a ﬁxed number of visual outputs as illustrated in Figure 4 (hence the name Resampler). The motivation for re-sampling the visual input to a ﬁxed and small number (in practice 64) of outputs is to signiﬁcantly reduce the computational complexity of vision-text cross attention, particularly important when dealing with multiple long videos. In similar spirit to Perceiver (Jaegle et al., 2021) and DETR (Carion et al., 2020), we learn a predeﬁned number of latent input queries. These latent queries are fed to a transformer stack and cross attend to the ﬂattened visual features

Unifying strong single-modal models. Training a multimodal vision and language model, starting from a pretrained LM, has the potential to save the immense computational resources used to train the LM in the ﬁrst place. However, a LM trained only on text has no built-in means of incorporating inputs from other modalities. Introducing such inputs to a pretrained LM is one challenge in our setting: it is crucial to keep the pretrained model’s language understanding and generation capabilities fully intact, avoiding any destabilising interventions, while still leveraging the model’s full capacity and depth on the inputs from the new modality. To address this diﬃculty, we propose to interleave cross-attention layers with regular language-only self-attention layers that are kept frozen during training. To minimize the eﬀect of these newly added layers at initialization, we introduce speciﬁc gating mechanisms which greatly improve stability and ﬁnal performance.

This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

• Due to the use of frozen unimodal models and a lightweight Q-Former, BLIP-2 is more compute-efﬁcient than exisiting state-of-the-arts. For example, BLIP-2 out- performs Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54× fewer trainable pa- rameters. Furthermore, our results show that BLIP-2 is a generic method that can harvest more advanced unimodal models for better VLP performance.

• BLIP-2 effectively leverages both frozen pre-trained im- age models and language models. We bridge the modality gap using a Q-Former pre-trained in two-stages: repre- sentation learning stage and generative learning stage. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks including visual question answer- ing, image captioning, and image-text retrieval.

In our experiments, we use 32 queries where each query has a dimension of 768 (same as the hidden dimension of the Q-Former). We use Z to denote the output query representation. The size of Z (32 × 768) is much smaller than the size of frozen image features (e.g. 257 × 1024 for ViT-L/14). This bottleneck architecture works together with our pre-training objectives into forcing the queries to extract visual information that is most relevant to the text.

• Powered by LLMs (e.g. OPT (Zhang et al., 2022), FlanT5 (Chung et al., 2022)), BLIP-2 can be prompted to perform zero-shot image-to-text generation that follows natural language instructions, which enables emerging capabilities such as visual knowledge reasoning, visual conversation, etc. (see Figure 4 for examples).

Flamingo bridges the frozen vision encoder and frozen LM via two learnable components: a Perceiver Resampler followed by freshly initialised cross-attention layers interleaved between the pretrained LM layers.
The Perceiver Resampler takes a variable number of image or video features from the vision encoder and produces a fixed, small number (64) of visual tokens via learned latent queries fed to a transformer stack that cross-attends to the flattened visual features, reducing the complexity of vision-text cross attention.

evidence.text: The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

Second, those visual tokens are used to condition the frozen LM using freshly initialised cross attention layers (Section 3.1.2) that are interleaved between the pretrained LM layers. These new layers oﬀer an expressive way for the LM to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.

Unifying strong single-modal models. Training a multimodal vision and language model, starting from a pretrained LM, has the potential to save the immense computational resources used to train the LM in the ﬁrst place. However, a LM trained only on text has no built-in means of incorporating inputs from other modalities. Introducing such inputs to a pretrained LM is one challenge in our setting: it is crucial to keep the pretrained model’s language understanding and generation capabilities fully intact, avoiding any destabilising interventions, while still leveraging the model’s full capacity and depth on the inputs from the new modality. To address this diﬃculty, we propose to interleave cross-attention layers with regular language-only self-attention layers that are kept frozen during training. To minimize the eﬀect of these newly added layers at initialization, we introduce speciﬁc gating mechanisms which greatly improve stability and ﬁnal performance.

This section describes our approach to building the Flamingo model: a visual language model that accepts text interleaved with images/videos as input and outputs free-form text. Despite its apparent simplicity, this API is suﬃciently expressive to tackle a diverse range of tasks. In particular, it handles both open-ended tasks such as visual question-answering or captioning, which require generating text, and close-ended tasks such as classiﬁcation, which require choosing the best category or answer amongst a set. Requirement: `req_d32044dbb8eac1c40906bd9749a65701` · Status: `verified`

Flamingo follows a two-stage recipe: first pretraining a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image objective and starting from an existing pretrained autoregressive LM, then a main training phase that attaches learnable bridge components while freezing the pretrained vision and language models.
Flamingo freezes the pretrained vision encoder (NFNet-F6) and keeps it frozen during the main training phase, freezes the pretrained LM weights so their initial capacity remains unchanged, and keeps the regular language-only self-attention layers frozen.
The trainable components are the newly added learnable architecture components: the Perceiver Resampler (with learnt latent queries) and the freshly initialised gated cross-attention layers interleaved between the frozen pretrained LM layers, which condition the LM on visual tokens.

evidence.text: Vision encoder: from pixels to features. Our model’s vision encoder is a pretrained Normalizer- Free ResNet (NFNet) (Brock et al., 2021) – we use the F6 model. We chose this family of visual backbones thanks to their excellent trade-oﬀbetween performance and eﬃciency given our hardware. We pretrain the vision encoder using a contrastive objective on our datasets of image and text pairs,

The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

Second, those visual tokens are used to condition the frozen LM using freshly initialised cross attention layers (Section 3.1.2) that are interleaved between the pretrained LM layers. These new layers oﬀer an expressive way for the LM to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.

Contrastive similarities are computed as the dot product of the mean pooling of the image encoder output, and the mean pooled output of a BERT model (Devlin et al., 2018). The performance of our contrastive pretrained model is given in Section 4.2.3 and more details about the contrastive training are given in Appendix C.2.2. During the main training phase of the Flamingo models, we leave the vision encoder frozen as it performs favorably when compared to training the vision model directly from our text generation objective (see ablations in Section 4.4). Unifying strong single-modal models. Training a multimodal vision and language model, starting from a pretrained LM, has the potential to save the immense computational resources used to train the LM in the ﬁrst place. However, a LM trained only on text has no built-in means of incorporating inputs from other modalities. Introducing such inputs to a pretrained LM is one challenge in our setting: it is crucial to keep the pretrained model’s language understanding and generation capabilities fully intact, avoiding any destabilising interventions, while still leveraging the model’s full capacity and depth on the inputs from the new modality. To address this diﬃculty, we propose to interleave cross-attention layers with regular language-only self-attention layers that are kept frozen during training. To minimize the eﬀect of these newly added layers at initialization, we introduce speciﬁc gating mechanisms which greatly improve stability and ﬁnal performance.

arguments.query: frozen image encoder frozen LLM trainable Q-Former two-stage training

evidence.text: Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

In the generative pre-training stage, we connect Q- Former (with the frozen image encoder attached) to a frozen LLM to harvest the LLM’s generative language capability. As shown in Figure 3, we use a fully-connected (FC) layer to linearly project the output query embeddings Z into the same dimension as the text embedding of the LLM. The projected query embeddings are then prepended to the input text embeddings. They function as soft visual prompts that condition the LLM on visual representation extracted by the Q-Former. Since the Q-Former has been pre-trained to extract language-informative visual representation, it ef- fectively functions as an information bottleneck that feeds the most useful information to the LLM while removing irrelevant visual information. This reduces the burden of the LLM to learn vision-language alignment, thus mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem.

In the representation learning stage, we connect Q-Former to a frozen image encoder and perform pre-training using image-text pairs. requirements.question: For the assigned paper only, provide its documented facts needed to address: Compare BLIP-2 and Flamingo on training objective using only the prepared corpus.
requirements.claim:
BLIP-2 pre-trains its Q-Former in two stages: a first vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder, and a second vision-to-language generative learning stage with a frozen LLM.
In the representation learning stage, three pre-training objectives inspired by BLIP are jointly optimized with shared input format and model parameters, each using a different attention masking strategy between queries and text to control their interaction.
The representation learning stage trains the Q-Former so its queries learn to extract visual representation most informative of the text, while the generative stage connects the Q-Former to a frozen LLM and uses projected query embeddings as soft visual prompts to condition the LLM on the Q-Former's visual representation.
The first (representation learning) stage jointly optimizes three pre-training objectives inspired by BLIP, sharing the same input format and model parameters, with each objective using a different query-text attention masking strategy.
The first stage aims to train the Q-Former such that its queries learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text, using image-text pairs with a frozen image encoder.
The second (generative pre-training) stage connects the Q-Former with frozen image encoder to a frozen LLM, projecting query embeddings via a fully-connected layer to the LLM text embedding dimension and prepending them as soft visual prompts.
The second stage harvests the frozen LLM's generative language capability, with the Q-Former acting as an information bottleneck that feeds useful visual information and mitigates catastrophic forgetting.

requirements.question: For the assigned paper only, provide its documented facts needed to address: Compare BLIP-2 and Flamingo on training objective using only the prepared corpus.
requirements.claim:
Flamingo's training is documented in two stages: a vision-encoder pretraining stage using a contrastive text-image approach à la CLIP, and a main training phase in which the pretrained frozen vision encoder and frozen LM are linked via newly initialised cross-attention layers and a Perceiver Resampler.
The vision-encoder pretraining stage uses the two-term contrastive loss from Radford et al. (2021) on image-text pairs, with contrastive similarities computed as the dot product of mean-pooled image encoder outputs and mean-pooled BERT outputs. The main training phase optimizes a text generation objective / next-token prediction task.
Flamingo freezes the pretrained vision encoder and the pretrained autoregressive LM weights during the main training phase, training only the newly added components (Perceiver Resampler and interleaved cross-attention layers) so that the pretrained models' initial capacity remains unchanged.
Vision encoder (NFNet-F6) is pretrained with a contrastive text-image objective à la CLIP, using the two-term contrastive loss from Radford et al. (2021) with dot-product similarities between mean-pooled image features and mean-pooled BERT text features.
Stage 1 optimizes the vision encoder and text encoder to extract semantic spatial features from image-text pairs via the contrastive objective.
Main Flamingo training uses a text generation (next-token prediction) objective, with the frozen LM conditioned on visual tokens via cross-attention to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.
In the main phase the vision encoder is left frozen (chosen over training it directly from the text generation objective) and the pretrained LM is frozen; only the newly initialised cross-attention layers and Perceiver Resampler are trained.

Flamingo's training is documented in two stages: a vision-encoder pretraining stage using a contrastive text-image approach à la CLIP, and a main training phase in which the pretrained frozen vision encoder and frozen LM are linked via newly initialised cross-attention layers and a Perceiver Resampler.
The vision-encoder pretraining stage uses the two-term contrastive loss from Radford et al. (2021) on image-text pairs, with contrastive similarities computed as the dot product of mean-pooled image encoder outputs and mean-pooled BERT outputs. The main training phase optimizes a text generation objective / next-token prediction task.
Flamingo freezes the pretrained vision encoder and the pretrained autoregressive LM weights during the main training phase, training only the newly added components (Perceiver Resampler and interleaved cross-attention layers) so that the pretrained models' initial capacity remains unchanged.
Vision encoder (NFNet-F6) is pretrained with a contrastive text-image objective à la CLIP, using the two-term contrastive loss from Radford et al. (2021) with dot-product similarities between mean-pooled image features and mean-pooled BERT text features.
Stage 1 optimizes the vision encoder and text encoder to extract semantic spatial features from image-text pairs via the contrastive objective.
Main Flamingo training uses a text generation (next-token prediction) objective, with the frozen LM conditioned on visual tokens via cross-attention to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.
In the main phase the vision encoder is left frozen (chosen over training it directly from the text generation objective) and the pretrained LM is frozen; only the newly initialised cross-attention layers and Perceiver Resampler are trained.

evidence.text: We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

The cost of vision-and-language pre-training has become increasingly prohibitive due to end-to- end training of large-scale models. This paper proposes BLIP-2, a generic and efﬁcient pre- training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language mod- els. BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a lightweight Querying Transformer, which is pre- trained in two stages. The ﬁrst stage boot- straps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision- language tasks, despite having signiﬁcantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer train- able parameters. We also demonstrate the model’s emerging capabilities of zero-shot image-to-text generation that can follow natural language in- structions.

• BLIP-2 effectively leverages both frozen pre-trained im- age models and language models. We bridge the modality gap using a Q-Former pre-trained in two-stages: repre- sentation learning stage and generative learning stage. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks including visual question answer- ing, image captioning, and image-text retrieval.

In the representation learning stage, we connect Q-Former to a frozen image encoder and perform pre-training using image-text pairs. We aim to train the Q-Former such that the queries can learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text. Inspired by BLIP (Li et al., 2022), we jointly optimize three pre-training objectives that share the same input format and model parameters. Each objec- tive employs a different attention masking strategy between queries and text to control their interaction (see Figure 2).

In the generative pre-training stage, we connect Q- Former (with the frozen image encoder attached) to a frozen LLM to harvest the LLM’s generative language capability. As shown in Figure 3, we use a fully-connected (FC) layer to linearly project the output query embeddings Z into the same dimension as the text embedding of the LLM. The projected query embeddings are then prepended to the input text embeddings. They function as soft visual prompts that condition the LLM on visual representation extracted by the Q-Former. Since the Q-Former has been pre-trained to extract language-informative visual representation, it ef- fectively functions as an information bottleneck that feeds the most useful information to the LLM while removing irrelevant visual information. This reduces the burden of the LLM to learn vision-language alignment, thus mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem.

evidence.text: The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

Unifying strong single-modal models. Training a multimodal vision and language model, starting from a pretrained LM, has the potential to save the immense computational resources used to train the LM in the ﬁrst place. However, a LM trained only on text has no built-in means of incorporating inputs from other modalities. Introducing such inputs to a pretrained LM is one challenge in our setting: it is crucial to keep the pretrained model’s language understanding and generation capabilities fully intact, avoiding any destabilising interventions, while still leveraging the model’s full capacity and depth on the inputs from the new modality. To address this diﬃculty, we propose to interleave cross-attention layers with regular language-only self-attention layers that are kept frozen during training. To minimize the eﬀect of these newly added layers at initialization, we introduce speciﬁc gating mechanisms which greatly improve stability and ﬁnal performance.

The ﬁrst stage boot- straps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer train- able parameters. The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

Unifying strong single-modal models. Training a multimodal vision and language model, starting from a pretrained LM, has the potential to save the immense computational resources used to train the LM in the ﬁrst place. However, a LM trained only on text has no built-in means of incorporating inputs from other modalities. Introducing such inputs to a pretrained LM is one challenge in our setting: it is crucial to keep the pretrained model’s language understanding and generation capabilities fully intact, avoiding any destabilising interventions, while still leveraging the model’s full capacity and depth on the inputs from the new modality. To address this diﬃculty, we propose to interleave cross-attention layers with regular language-only self-attention layers that are kept frozen during training. To minimize the eﬀect of these newly added layers at initialization, we introduce speciﬁc gating mechanisms which greatly improve stability and ﬁnal performance.

Second, those visual tokens are used to condition the frozen LM using freshly initialised cross attention layers (Section 3.1.2) that are interleaved between the pretrained LM layers. These new layers oﬀer an expressive way for the LM to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.

evidence.text: Pre-training settings. We pre-train for 250k steps in the ﬁrst stage and 80k steps in the second stage. We use a batch size of 2320/1680 for ViT-L/ViT-G in the ﬁrst stage and a batch size of 1920/1520 for OPT/FlanT5 in the second stage. During pre-training, we convert the frozen ViTs’ and LLMs’ parameters into FP16, except for FlanT5 where we use BFloat16. We found no performance degradation compared to using 32-bit models. Due to the use of frozen models, our pre-training is more computational friendly than existing large-scale VLP methods. For example, using a single 16-A100(40G) machine, our largest model with ViT-G and FlanT5-XXL requires less than 6 days for the ﬁrst stage and less than 3 days for the second stage.

In the representation learning stage, we connect Q-Former to a frozen image encoder and perform pre-training using image-text pairs. We aim to train the Q-Former such that the queries can learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text. Inspired by BLIP (Li et al., 2022), we jointly optimize three pre-training objectives that share the same input format and model parameters. Each objec- tive employs a different attention masking strategy between queries and text to control their interaction (see Figure 2).

The cost of vision-and-language pre-training has become increasingly prohibitive due to end-to- end training of large-scale models. This paper proposes BLIP-2, a generic and efﬁcient pre- training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language mod- els. BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a lightweight Querying Transformer, which is pre- trained in two stages. The ﬁrst stage boot- straps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision- language tasks, despite having signiﬁcantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer train- able parameters. We also demonstrate the model’s emerging capabilities of zero-shot image-to-text generation that can follow natural language in- structions.

• BLIP-2 effectively leverages both frozen pre-trained im- age models and language models. We bridge the modality gap using a Q-Former pre-trained in two-stages: repre- sentation learning stage and generative learning stage. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks including visual question answer- ing, image captioning, and image-text retrieval.

We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

Despite its apparent simplicity, this API is suﬃciently expressive to tackle a diverse range of tasks. evidence.text: In our experiments, we use 32 queries where each query has a dimension of 768 (same as the hidden dimension of the Q-Former). We use Z to denote the output query representation. The size of Z (32 × 768) is much smaller than the size of frozen image features (e.g. 257 × 1024 for ViT-L/14). This bottleneck architecture works together with our pre-training objectives into forcing the queries to extract visual information that is most relevant to the text.

In the generative pre-training stage, we connect Q- Former (with the frozen image encoder attached) to a frozen LLM to harvest the LLM’s generative language capability. As shown in Figure 3, we use a fully-connected (FC) layer to linearly project the output query embeddings Z into the same dimension as the text embedding of the LLM. The projected query embeddings are then prepended to the input text embeddings. They function as soft visual prompts that condition the LLM on visual representation extracted by the Q-Former. Since the Q-Former has been pre-trained to extract language-informative visual representation, it ef- fectively functions as an information bottleneck that feeds the most useful information to the LLM while removing irrelevant visual information. This reduces the burden of the LLM to learn vision-language alignment, thus mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem.

verified_claims.text:
BLIP-2 explores the unsupervised-trained OPT model family for decoder-based LLMs and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family for encoder-decoder-based LLMs as its frozen language models.
BLIP-2 experiments with two types of LLM architectures: decoder-based LLMs (OPT) pre-trained with the language modeling loss, and encoder-decoder-based LLMs (FlanT5) pre-trained with the prefix language modeling loss.
The language models are kept frozen: BLIP-2 bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen LLM, and the frozen LLM is tasked to generate text conditioned on the visual representation from Q-Former.

evidence.text: Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

• Powered by LLMs (e.g. OPT (Zhang et al., 2022), FlanT5 (Chung et al., 2022)), BLIP-2 can be prompted to perform zero-shot image-to-text generation that follows natural language instructions, which enables emerging capabilities such as visual knowledge reasoning, visual conversation, etc. (see Figure 4 for examples).

We experiment with two types of LLMs: decoder-based LLMs and encoder-decoder-based LLMs. For decoder- based LLMs, we pre-train with the language modeling loss, where the frozen LLM is tasked to generate the text con- ditioned on the visual representation from Q-Former. For encoder-decoder-based LLMs, we pre-train with the preﬁx language modeling loss, where we split a text into two parts. The preﬁx text is concatenated with the visual representation as input to the LLM’s encoder. The sufﬁx text is used as the generation target for the LLM’s decoder.

The cost of vision-and-language pre-training has become increasingly prohibitive due to end-to- end training of large-scale models. This paper proposes BLIP-2, a generic and efﬁcient pre- training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language mod- els. BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a lightweight Querying Transformer, which is pre- trained in two stages. The ﬁrst stage boot- straps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision- language tasks, despite having signiﬁcantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer train- able parameters. We also demonstrate the model’s emerging capabilities of zero-shot image-to-text generation that can follow natural language in- structions.

We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

verified_claims.text:
Flamingo starts from an existing pretrained autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoffmann et al., 2022), gaining strong generative language abilities and access to knowledge stored in the LM weights.
Visual tokens condition the frozen LM via freshly initialized cross-attention layers interleaved between the pretrained LM layers, alongside regular language-only self-attention layers.
The weights of the pretrained LM are frozen so that their initial capacity remains unchanged; only gated cross-attention layers added to the LM are trained.

evidence.text: The architectural components shown in Figure 3 are key to the performance of Flamingo models, and these are chosen according to two objectives. The ﬁrst objective is to leverage pretrained models without having to spend compute training them from scratch. On the vision side, we pretrain a vision encoder with a contrastive text-image approach, à la CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). The role of this model is to extract semantic spatial features that describe attributes that one would want to query about a visual datum: color, shape, nature, positions of objects, etc. On the language side, we start from an existing autoregressive language model (LM) trained on a large and diverse text corpus (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). By doing so, Flamingo models gain strong generative language abilities and access to a large amount of knowledge stored in the LM weights. The second objective is to bridge these pretrained models harmoniously. To do so, we freeze the weights of these models so that their initial capacity remains unchanged. We then link them via two learnable architecture components. First, the Perceiver Resampler (Section 3.1.1) receives spatio-temporal features from the Vision Encoder (obtained from either image or video) and outputs a ﬁxed-size set of visual tokens.

Second, those visual tokens are used to condition the frozen LM using freshly initialised cross attention layers (Section 3.1.2) that are interleaved between the pretrained LM layers. These new layers oﬀer an expressive way for the LM to incorporate visual information for the next-token prediction task.

Unifying strong single-modal models. Training a multimodal vision and language model, starting from a pretrained LM, has the potential to save the immense computational resources used to train the LM in the ﬁrst place. However, a LM trained only on text has no built-in means of incorporating inputs from other modalities. Introducing such inputs to a pretrained LM is one challenge in our setting: it is crucial to keep the pretrained model’s language understanding and generation capabilities fully intact, avoiding any destabilising interventions, while still leveraging the model’s full capacity and depth on the inputs from the new modality. To address this diﬃculty, we propose to interleave cross-attention layers with regular language-only self-attention layers that are kept frozen during training. To minimize the eﬀect of these newly added layers at initialization, we introduce speciﬁc gating mechanisms which greatly improve stability and ﬁnal performance.

This section describes our approach to building the Flamingo model: a visual language model that accepts text interleaved with images/videos as input and outputs free-form text. Despite its apparent simplicity, this API is suﬃciently expressive to tackle a diverse range of tasks. In particular, it handles both open-ended tasks such as visual question-answering or captioning, which require generating text, and close-ended tasks such as classiﬁcation, which require choosing the best category or answer amongst a set. The cost of vision-and-language pre-training has become increasingly prohibitive due to end-to- end training of large-scale models. This paper proposes BLIP-2, a generic and efﬁcient pre- training strategy that bootstraps vision-language pre-training from off-the-shelf frozen pre-trained image encoders and frozen large language mod- els. BLIP-2 bridges the modality gap with a lightweight Querying Transformer, which is pre- trained in two stages. The ﬁrst stage boot- straps vision-language representation learning from a frozen image encoder. The second stage bootstraps vision-to-language generative learning from a frozen language model. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision- language tasks, despite having signiﬁcantly fewer trainable parameters than existing methods. For example, our model outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54x fewer train- able parameters. We also demonstrate the model’s emerging capabilities of zero-shot image-to-text generation that can follow natural language in- structions.

We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

evidence.text: In our experiments, we use 32 queries where each query has a dimension of 768 (same as the hidden dimension of the Q-Former). We use Z to denote the output query representation. The size of Z (32 × 768) is much smaller than the size of frozen image features (e.g. 257 × 1024 for ViT-L/14). This bottleneck architecture works together with our pre-training objectives into forcing the queries to extract visual information that is most relevant to the text.

In the representation learning stage, we connect Q-Former to a frozen image encoder and perform pre-training using image-text pairs. We aim to train the Q-Former such that the queries can learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text. Inspired by BLIP (Li et al., 2022), we jointly optimize three pre-training objectives that share the same input format and model parameters. Each objec- tive employs a different attention masking strategy between queries and text to control their interaction (see Figure 2).

evidence.text: Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

Pre-training settings. We pre-train for 250k steps in the ﬁrst stage and 80k steps in the second stage. We use a batch size of 2320/1680 for ViT-L/ViT-G in the ﬁrst stage and a batch size of 1920/1520 for OPT/FlanT5 in the second stage. During pre-training, we convert the frozen ViTs’ and LLMs’ parameters into FP16, except for FlanT5 where we use BFloat16. We found no performance degradation compared to using 32-bit models. Due to the use of frozen models, our pre-training is more computational friendly than existing large-scale VLP methods. For example, using a single 16-A100(40G) machine, our largest model with ViT-G and FlanT5-XXL requires less than 6 days for the ﬁrst stage and less than 3 days for the second stage.

• Powered by LLMs (e.g. OPT (Zhang et al., 2022), FlanT5 (Chung et al., 2022)), BLIP-2 can be prompted to perform zero-shot image-to-text generation that follows natural language instructions, which enables emerging capabilities such as visual knowledge reasoning, visual conversation, etc. (see Figure 4 for examples).

We experiment with two types of LLMs: decoder-based LLMs and encoder-decoder-based LLMs. For decoder- based LLMs, we pre-train with the language modeling loss, where the frozen LLM is tasked to generate the text con- ditioned on the visual representation from Q-Former. For encoder-decoder-based LLMs, we pre-train with the preﬁx language modeling loss, where we split a text into two parts. The preﬁx text is concatenated with the visual representation as input to the LLM’s encoder. The sufﬁx text is used as the generation target for the LLM’s decoder.

• Due to the use of frozen unimodal models and a lightweight Q-Former, BLIP-2 is more compute-efﬁcient than exisiting state-of-the-arts. For example, BLIP-2 out- performs Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54× fewer trainable pa- rameters. Furthermore, our results show that BLIP-2 is a generic method that can harvest more advanced unimodal models for better VLP performance.

evidence.text: We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

In the generative pre-training stage, we connect Q- Former (with the frozen image encoder attached) to a frozen LLM to harvest the LLM’s generative language capability. As shown in Figure 3, we use a fully-connected (FC) layer to linearly project the output query embeddings Z into the same dimension as the text embedding of the LLM. The projected query embeddings are then prepended to the input text embeddings. They function as soft visual prompts that condition the LLM on visual representation extracted by the Q-Former. Since the Q-Former has been pre-trained to extract language-informative visual representation, it ef- fectively functions as an information bottleneck that feeds the most useful information to the LLM while removing irrelevant visual information. This reduces the burden of the LLM to learn vision-language alignment, thus mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem.

In the representation learning stage, we connect Q-Former to a frozen image encoder and perform pre-training using image-text pairs. We aim to train the Q-Former such that the queries can learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text. Inspired by BLIP (Li et al., 2022), we jointly optimize three pre-training objectives that share the same input format and model parameters. Each objec- tive employs a different attention masking strategy between queries and text to control their interaction (see Figure 2).

evidence.text: • Due to the use of frozen unimodal models and a lightweight Q-Former, BLIP-2 is more compute-efﬁcient than exisiting state-of-the-arts. For example, BLIP-2 out- performs Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54× fewer trainable pa- rameters. Furthermore, our results show that BLIP-2 is a generic method that can harvest more advanced unimodal models for better VLP performance.

• BLIP-2 effectively leverages both frozen pre-trained im- age models and language models. We bridge the modality gap using a Q-Former pre-trained in two-stages: repre- sentation learning stage and generative learning stage. BLIP-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various vision-language tasks including visual question answer- ing, image captioning, and image-text retrieval.

In the representation learning stage, we connect Q-Former to a frozen image encoder and perform pre-training using image-text pairs. We aim to train the Q-Former such that the queries can learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text. Inspired by BLIP (Li et al., 2022), we jointly optimize three pre-training objectives that share the same input format and model parameters. Each objec- tive employs a different attention masking strategy between queries and text to control their interaction (see Figure 2).

We propose BLIP-2, a new vision-language pre-training method that bootstraps from frozen pre-trained unimodal models. In order to bridge the modality gap, we propose a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) pre-trained in two stages: (1) vision-language representation learning stage with a frozen image encoder and (2) vision-to-language genera- tive learning stage with a frozen LLM. This section ﬁrst introduces the model architecture of Q-Former, and then delineates the two-stage pre-training procedures.

Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. For the frozen im- age encoder, we explore two state-of-the-art pre-trained vision transformer models: (1) ViT-L/14 from CLIP (Rad- ford et al., 2021) and (2) ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP (Fang et al., 2022). We remove the last layer of the ViT and uses the second last layer’s output features, which leads to slightly better performance. For the frozen language model, we explore the unsupervised-trained OPT model family (Zhang et al., 2022) for decoder-based LLMs, and the instruction-trained FlanT5 model family (Chung et al., 2022) for encoder-decoder-based LLMs.

evidence.text: Pre-trained image encoder and LLM. We experiment with two types of LLMs: decoder-based LLMs and encoder-decoder-based LLMs. For decoder- based LLMs, we pre-train with the language modeling loss, where the frozen LLM is tasked to generate the text con- ditioned on the visual representation from Q-Former. For encoder-decoder-based LLMs, we pre-train with the preﬁx language modeling loss, where we split a text into two parts. The preﬁx text is concatenated with the visual representation as input to the LLM’s encoder. The sufﬁx text is used as the generation target for the LLM’s decoder.

Pre-training settings. We pre-train for 250k steps in the ﬁrst stage and 80k steps in the second stage. We use a batch size of 2320/1680 for ViT-L/ViT-G in the ﬁrst stage and a batch size of 1920/1520 for OPT/FlanT5 in the second stage. During pre-training, we convert the frozen ViTs’ and LLMs’ parameters into FP16, except for FlanT5 where we use BFloat16. We found no performance degradation compared to using 32-bit models. Due to the use of frozen models, our pre-training is more computational friendly than existing large-scale VLP methods. For example, using a single 16-A100(40G) machine, our largest model with ViT-G and FlanT5-XXL requires less than 6 days for the ﬁrst stage and less than 3 days for the second stage.

• Due to the use of frozen unimodal models and a lightweight Q-Former, BLIP-2 is more compute-efﬁcient than exisiting state-of-the-arts. For example, BLIP-2 out- performs Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54× fewer trainable pa- rameters. Furthermore, our results show that BLIP-2 is a generic method that can harvest more advanced unimodal models for better VLP performance.

In the generative pre-training stage, we connect Q- Former (with the frozen image encoder attached) to a frozen LLM to harvest the LLM’s generative language capability. As shown in Figure 3, we use a fully-connected (FC) layer to linearly project the output query embeddings Z into the same dimension as the text embedding of the LLM. The projected query embeddings are then prepended to the input text embeddings. They function as soft visual prompts that condition the LLM on visual representation extracted by the Q-Former. Since the Q-Former has been pre-trained to extract language-informative visual representation, it ef- fectively functions as an information bottleneck that feeds the most useful information to the LLM while removing irrelevant visual information. This reduces the burden of the LLM to learn vision-language alignment, thus mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem.

Instruction tuning large language models (LLMs) using machine-generated instruction-following data has improved zero-shot capabilities on new tasks, but the idea is less explored in the multimodal ﬁeld. In this paper, we present the ﬁrst attempt to use language-only GPT-4 to generate multimodal language-image instruction-following data. By instruction tuning on such generated data, we in- troduce LLaVA: Large Language and Vision Assistant, an end-to-end trained large multimodal model that connects a vision encoder and LLM for general- purpose visual and language understanding. Our early experiments show that LLaVA demonstrates impressive multimodel chat abilities, sometimes exhibiting the behaviors of multimodal GPT-4 on unseen images/instructions, and yields a 85.1% relative score compared with GPT-4 on a synthetic multimodal instruction- following dataset. When ﬁne-tuned on Science QA, the synergy of LLaVA and GPT-4 achieves a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 92.53%. We make GPT-4 gener- ated visual instruction tuning data, our model and code base publicly available.
